title: How to communicate clinical trial results to physicians
overview: How to communicate clinical trial results to physicians: clinical evidence communication, clinical data visualisation and medical education video that cardiologists act on.
author: Made Clear
body:
Knowing how to communicate clinical trial results to physicians can decide whether a therapy is adopted or ignored. Physicians are trained to scrutinise data, and they hear about new trials constantly. Results that are buried in a slide deck, or overstated in a brochure, rarely change practice. Results explained clearly, honestly and by the right people can.

Here's what we've learned about clinical evidence communication from working with medtech teams across cardiology.

Lead with the clinical question

Physicians don't start with the endpoint; they start with the patient in front of them. Frame the results around the question the trial answers: which patients, compared with what, and what difference it makes. Then show the data that supports it.

Tell the story behind the data

Trial results land best when physicians understand where they fit. When Medtronic needed to rebuild confidence in renal denervation after disappointing earlier results, the answer wasn't just the new data. Our HTN:RDN programme began with a four-part documentary that retold the history of the therapy, including what went wrong, before the new results were announced. That context made the new evidence credible.

  • Acknowledge earlier results honestly, including the disappointing ones.
  • Explain what changed in the trial design or the technology.
  • Let the investigators explain the findings in their own words.

Be there when the results are announced

Major trial results are usually presented at congresses, and the conversation starts the moment they're shown. For HTN:RDN, we provided live coverage of the pivotal trial results at the ACC congress, so the key messages reached physicians while the field was still discussing them. Interviews with investigators filmed on the day can be shared within hours.

Clinical data visualisation

Good clinical data visualisation makes a result understandable at a glance, without distorting it.

  • One message per chart. Show the comparison that matters, not every secondary endpoint at once.
  • Keep the scale honest. Truncated axes and selective timeframes are noticed and resented.
  • Show uncertainty. Confidence intervals and patient numbers build trust rather than weakening the message.
  • Animate with care. Motion can guide the eye through a result step by step, but it should never exaggerate it.
  • Connect data to anatomy. Showing what is happening inside the vessel makes the numbers mean something.

Medical education video

A medical education video lets a respected physician explain the data, show the technique and discuss what it means for patient selection. It's often far more effective than a written summary, because physicians hear the evidence from a peer.

For The Calcium Masterclass, we produced a 10-part programme with Shockwave Medical and Optima Education to educate US interventional cardiologists about intravascular lithotripsy on the eve of FDA approval. Over 5,500 cardiologists took part, spending an average of 28 minutes each, and the programme helped Shockwave dramatically reduce the time from product launch to adoption.

Medical affairs content and compliance

Medical affairs content has to be balanced, accurate and compliant, which can make it cautious and dry. It doesn't have to be. Physicians respond to clarity and to the honest discussion of limitations. Involve medical and regulatory reviewers early, agree what can and can't be said, and build the content around that, rather than trying to soften claims at the end.

Plan for the long term

A trial result is not a single announcement. Physicians need to hear it more than once, in different formats, from different voices. The HTN:RDN programme ran for two years, with a sustained expert-led education programme and local versions in six languages. It reached 4 million healthcare professionals, drove 117k content views and a fivefold increase in searches for renal denervation. By 2022, 12 leading hypertension societies had reached a consensus supporting renal denervation as a complementary therapy.

A simple checklist

  • What clinical question does the trial answer, and for which patients?
  • Which investigators and KOLs will explain it?
  • How will the key result be visualised honestly?
  • What happens on the day of the announcement?
  • How will the message be repeated and localised over the following months?
